tasks.prompt: The graph below shows the percentage of electricity generated from four different sources in one country between 2000 and 2020.
tasks.instructions: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Share of electricity generated by source, 2000–2020

tasks.modelAnswer:
The line graph illustrates how the proportion of electricity produced from coal, natural gas, nuclear power and renewable sources changed in one country over the two decades from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, the most striking development was the replacement of coal by renewables as the leading source of electricity. Natural gas grew moderately, while the share of nuclear power declined slightly throughout the period.

In 2000, coal was by far the dominant fuel, accounting for just over half (52%) of all electricity generated, whereas renewables contributed a mere 5%. Over the following twenty years, however, these two sources moved in opposite directions. Coal fell gradually at first and then more sharply after 2010, ending the period at only 12%. Renewables, by contrast, rose slowly until 2010 before accelerating dramatically to reach 43% in 2020, overtaking every other source.

The figure for natural gas climbed from 28% to a peak of 38% in 2015, making it the largest single source in that year, before dipping to 34% by the end of the period. Nuclear power remained relatively stable, edging down by one percentage point every five years from 15% to 11%.
tips: Start with a one-sentence paraphrase of the prompt, then give an overview of the two or three biggest trends (here: coal replaced by renewables; gas up slightly; nuclear stable) without numbers.
Group the data instead of describing each line year by year: the two lines that cross (coal and renewables) make a natural body paragraph, the two flatter lines another.
Support every comparison with exact figures and years, and vary your language: 'fell sharply', 'edged down', 'peaked at', 'overtook'.
Do not explain why the changes happened or give opinions — Task 1 only reports what the chart shows.

tasks.prompt:
Some people believe that university education should be free for every student, paid for by the government. Others think that students should pay the cost of their own studies, since they are the ones who benefit most.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
tasks.instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
tasks.modelAnswer:
How higher education should be funded is a question that governments everywhere continue to debate. While there are reasonable arguments for asking students to pay their own fees, I believe that university education should be largely free, because its benefits extend far beyond the individual graduate.

Those who favour tuition fees argue that graduates are the main beneficiaries of a degree. Over a working life, a university graduate typically earns considerably more than someone without one, so it seems fair that they, rather than taxpayers who may never have attended university, should bear the cost. Supporters also claim that paying fees makes students more committed, since they are less likely to drop out of a course for which they have made a significant financial sacrifice.

However, this view overlooks the wider value of an educated population. Society as a whole depends on doctors, engineers and teachers, and a country that trains more of them becomes more productive and better able to compete internationally. Moreover, high fees discourage talented young people from poorer families, who are often unwilling to take on large debts. The result is that university places go to those who can afford them rather than those who would benefit most, which is both unjust and wasteful. Graduates already contribute more through the tax system because of their higher earnings, so in effect they repay the cost of their education over time.

In conclusion, although the argument that graduates should pay for their own advantage has some logic, I am convinced that free university education is the better policy. It widens opportunity, rewards ability rather than wealth, and produces benefits that the whole community shares.
tips: In a 'discuss both views' question, give each view its own body paragraph and develop it fully, then make your own position clear in the introduction and conclusion.
Support each main point with a reason and a concrete consequence or example (e.g. talented students from poorer families avoiding debt).
Use linking language that signals your stance, such as 'However, this view overlooks…' or 'I am convinced that…', so the examiner can follow your argument.
Leave 3–5 minutes to check verb forms, articles and plurals — small repeated errors keep otherwise strong essays below Band 7.
